**Title:** Same Name, Different Unit: Identifying Source-Specific Units in Web Price Fusion

**Abstract (298 words):**

Web services that fuse values from many sources, such as price aggregators, indexes and oracles, assume that sources with the same unit name share one backing. Often they do not: a platform's ledger balance can carry the name of a common unit, the dollar, without its backing, and fusion reads a shift in that backing as a change in value. We model each source's values as true values plus a source-unit offset shared by all its items. Agreement across unrelated items identifies the offset, and a unit anchor, an item fixed in the true unit, separates a unit shift from demand. We formalise the test with an identification result, a GMM over-identification test and a calibrated simulation of size and power. On cryptocurrency exchanges, whose dollars are ledger claims, it gives the first test of a reading that Flowerday et al. (2026) say cannot be tested directly. Netting Tether's external price from Kraken out of Bitfinex's USDT/USD price makes it track Bitfinex's offset with slope close to one (0.97, 95% interval 0.94 to 1.00, up from 0.71). Bitfinex's 2018 to 2019 premium was therefore two discounts, one on the ledger dollar and one on Tether. Binance.US in 2023 was a pure ledger-dollar shift (slope 1.00). On assets withheld from development, one offset per source-hour removed most of the gap in the stress years and, by the median year (0.389) and median asset (0.378), about a third to two-fifths in calm years. Across three locked fusion tests, a plain median was hard to beat. Unit-aware fusion won when a large group of sources shared a unit that moved by more than venue noise (the USDC 2023 test, error 0.72 of the median's) and not otherwise. Aggregators should correct when a shared unit can move and otherwise keep the median.

**Suggested keywords:** exchange dollars; unit of account; truth discovery; price feeds and oracles; Web data quality; cryptocurrency markets; reproducibility
